passage:
Trisha: I can't stop hearing this voice. It says you're worthless
Deepika: Oh Trish. What happened?
Trisha: I forgot to upload our group's final file. The deadline passed. Three of us lost marks because of me
Deepika: That's a serious mistake. It's also one mistake. The voice is shame, not a fact about you
Trisha: It feels like a fact
Deepika: I know. What would you say to me if I'd done it?
Trisha: That I'd messed up and could still fix it
Deepika: So say that to yourself
Trisha: ...ok. I'll write to the professor tonight and explain, and tell the other two myself first
Deepika: I'll sit with you while you write it

qa.q: What did Trisha forget to do?
qa.a: Trisha forgot to upload the group's final file.

qa.q: What is Trisha feeling as the voice keeps repeating itself?
qa.a: Deep shame, since the voice saying worthless feels like a fact.

qa.q: What did Trisha decide to do about the mistake?
qa.a: Trisha decided to tell the other two directly first and then write to the professor to explain, which owns the harm and repairs it.

qa.q: How might the two teammates feel when Trisha tells them directly?
qa.a: They may feel disappointed about the marks, but respected for being told directly rather than finding out later.

grounding: After a serious mistake the protagonist hears a voice saying worthless; with a friend the mistake is separated from the self, the harm is owned and a repair is planned.

passage:
Dear Deepika,

I've started this letter six times. Last Thursday I forwarded your private message about your family to the whole project group by mistake, and then, when you asked, I lied and said someone hacked my phone. That second part is what I can't forgive myself for.

Since then there's a voice in my head all day: you're worthless, you're a terrible person. I stopped eating properly. I almost stopped coming to class so I wouldn't have to see you.

But hiding isn't fair to you. So here is the truth. I forwarded it. I lied because I was ashamed. I'm sorry for both.

I've asked everyone in the group to delete it, and I've told our professor what happened, in case anyone misuses it. I did a bad thing. I'm trying to be someone who doesn't repeat it.

Siddharth

qa.q: What did Siddharth forward by mistake?
qa.a: Siddharth forwarded Deepika's private message about family matters to the whole project group.

qa.q: What has Siddharth been feeling since last Thursday?
qa.a: Siddharth has felt deep shame and self-hatred, hearing a voice that says worthless, and wanted to hide.

qa.q: How is Siddharth trying to repair the harm?
qa.a: Siddharth tells the truth, apologises for both the mistake and the lie, asked the group to delete the message, and told the professor.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Deepika may still be hurt and angry, but the honest apology and repair steps could help Deepika trust a little again.

grounding: The letter shows a young person hearing a voice of worthlessness after a serious mistake, separating the act from the self, owning the harm and repairing it.

passage:
Jasleen, you asked about the worst week of my college life. It's Tushar speaking, so be kind. Second year, I was the mess secretary. I forgot to renew the gas cylinder order. On a Friday night two hundred students had no dinner. People were furious. Someone wrote my name on the notice board with a cross through it.

That night I lay awake and the voice was loud: you're useless, you're a waste of space, everyone hates you. I thought about quitting, not just the post, college.

My warden called me in the next morning. He said, "You made a serious mistake. You're not a serious mistake." Separating those two changed everything.

So I owned it. I apologised in the mess, in front of everyone. I set up a shared order calendar with two other students so it couldn't depend on one person. And I talked to myself like I'd talk to my younger brother. Firm, but kind.

qa.q: How many students had no dinner that Friday night?
qa.a: Two hundred students had no dinner.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling the night after the mistake?
qa.a: Tushar felt ashamed and worthless, hearing a harsh voice and thinking about quitting college.

qa.q: How did Tushar repair the harm?
qa.a: Tushar apologised publicly in the mess, set up a shared order calendar so it wouldn't happen again, and used firm but kind self-talk.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Tushar's mistake?
qa.a: The warden saw it as a serious error but not a judgement on Tushar's worth, helping Tushar separate the act from the person.

grounding: The monologue shows a young person who hears "you are worthless" after a serious mistake, separating the act from the self, owning the harm and repairing it.
